content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain bread is a whole‑grain loaf made from a blend of different cereals, seeds, and sometimes nuts. It has a dense crumb, a nutty‑seed aroma, and higher fiber and nutrient content compared with regular white bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix can include wheat, rye, barley, oats, sunflower, pumpkin and flax seeds.
Multigrain bread often contains more B‑vitamins and minerals such as iron and magnesium.
Flax seeds add a source of omega‑3 fatty acids.
Traditionally it is baked in stone ovens, giving the crust a crisp, crunchy texture.
Many countries have their own versions, e.g., Scandinavian “rød” or Italian “pan di campani”.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: High dietary fiber improves digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide a steadier blood‑sugar level than white bread.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B3 and folate support energy metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals and antioxidants
items.content: Magnesium, iron, zinc and seed antioxidants help boost immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole grains give the loaf a lower GI, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Allergy to grain or seeds
items.content: Some individuals may react to wheat, rye or seeds such as sunflower or pumpkin.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid this bread.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Certain varieties may contain added salt or preservatives; choose a plain, additive‑free version when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Multigrain bread works well for toast, sandwiches, and as a side for soups and salads. Toast it, spread avocado, cottage cheese or hummus, or pair with cheese, ham and vegetable fillings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag – it stays fresh for up to 2 months. Thaw in the oven or toaster before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Jelly roll cake is a light sponge roll filled with fruit jelly and often topped with a glaze. The batter is made from eggs, sugar, flour, and a small amount of leavening, baked as a thin sheet, spread with jelly, and rolled into a cylindrical shape.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The jelly roll originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became a party favorite.
Traditional fillings use berry jelly, but variations with cream, fruit puree, or chocolate are common.
The name comes from the English word “roll,” not from “jellybean.”
In some countries the dessert is called a “Swiss roll” or “biscuit roll.”
The thin sponge layer helps the roll keep its shape even after slicing.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The thin sponge contains little fat, especially when minimal butter or oil is used in the batter.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain flour provide riboflavin (B2), pyridoxine (B6) and folate.

items.title: Fruit jelly
items.content: Berry jelly adds vitamin C and antioxidants.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The cake is light and can serve as a quick post‑workout snack.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Both the jelly and the sponge often contain high amounts of sugar, which may be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Egg and gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use eggs and wheat flour, making the cake unsuitable for those with related allergies.

items.title: Acidity of jelly
items.content: Sour jelly can irritate a sensitive stomach in some individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the jelly roll chilled, sliced into portions. It can be garnished with fresh berries, whipped cream, or a dusting of powdered sugar. Pairs well with tea or a light dessert wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake refrigerated, wrapped in plastic film or stored in an airtight container, for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze the sliced portions.

content.title: About
content.content: The chicken fillet sandwich is a fast‑food item featuring a tender chicken breast, either grilled or fried, placed between a soft bun and often complemented with lettuce, sauce, and cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The chicken fillet is usually skinless, making it less fatty than many other fast‑food meats.
The grilled version is considered healthier because it requires little to no oil.
Chicken fillet sandwiches are commonly served in combo meals with fries and a drink.
Some regions add spices such as paprika or garlic to boost the fillet’s flavor.
Chicken breast is a good source of protein, B‑vitamins, and selenium.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat (grilled)
items.content: Grilling uses minimal added fat, making the sandwich a lighter option.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, helping protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and carbohydrates in the bun helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sauces and seasonings can add a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Fat in fried version
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calories and may introduce trans fats.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked fillet can harbor salmonella; internal temperature should reach 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is typically eaten by hand, sometimes split in half. It can be customized with fresh vegetables, mustard, mayo, or a yogurt‑based sauce. For a lighter choice, opt for grilled fillet and a whole‑grain bun.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed immediately. If you need to store it, wrap tightly in plastic film and keep refrigerated for no more than 24 hours. For longer storage, keep the chicken fillet separate in an airtight container at 0‑4 °C.

egg-sandwich-on-bagel-with-ham.title: Egg sandwich on bagel with ham

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich on a bagel with ham is a satisfying breakfast or snack consisting of a fresh bagel, a fried egg, and a slice of cooked ham. The blend of protein, fat, and carbohydrates provides lasting fullness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bagel originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine but is now enjoyed worldwide.
Eggs in the sandwich are often cooked sunny‑side‑up so the yolk stays runny.
The ham used is typically smoked, giving the sandwich its distinctive aroma.
The sandwich is portable and can be wrapped in paper or placed in a container for on‑the‑go meals.
The combination of egg and ham makes the dish a rich source of vitamin B12.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Egg and ham together provide about 20 g of protein, essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both ingredients contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Ham supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Energy sustaining
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bagel give quick energy, while protein and fat provide a slower release.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Ham contains monounsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly when eaten in moderation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed ham is often salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Large amounts of ham can increase saturated fat intake, affecting cholesterol levels.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The bagel and ham make the sandwich relatively calorie‑dense; consider it within daily energy needs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel in half, lightly toast it, place the fried egg and a slice of ham inside. Add lettuce, tomato, or mustard if desired. The sandwich can be eaten by hand or cut into bite‑size pieces for children.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. Keep bagels in a dry place, and ham wrapped tightly in the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: Fatty fish are species that store oils in their tissues and around the gut, giving them rich flavor and a soft, flaky texture. Common examples include salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring, trout, and anchovies. They are eaten fresh, smoked, canned, or cured in many cuisines around the world and are especially known for their omega-3 fatty acid content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Unlike lean white fish, fatty fish store oil throughout their flesh.
The omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA are found mainly in fatty fish and other seafood.
Many dietary guidelines suggest eating fish, including fatty fish, once or twice a week.
Sardines are often eaten whole, including their soft bones, which adds calcium.
Canned fatty fish such as sardines and mackerel are convenient and long-lasting.

items.title: Rich in omega-3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support normal heart function and brain function.

items.title: Source of high-quality protein
items.content: Fatty fish provide complete protein for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Provides vitamin D
items.content: Fatty fish are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12 and minerals
items.content: They provide vitamin B12, selenium, and iodine.

items.title: May support heart health
items.content: Some studies suggest that regular fish consumption is associated with better cardiovascular health, although more research is needed.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Fish allergy can be serious and is lifelong for many people.

items.title: Mercury and contaminants
items.content: Some larger fish may contain more mercury and other contaminants. Pregnant women and young children should follow local guidance on which fish to choose.

items.title: Raw or undercooked fish
items.content: Raw or undercooked fish may carry parasites and bacteria and is not recommended for pregnant women, young children, or people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: High doses of omega-3 supplements may affect blood clotting. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fatty fish can be baked, grilled, pan-seared, steamed, or poached. Smoked or cured fish is often eaten on bread or in salads, and canned fish can be added to sandwiches, pasta, or salads. Cook fresh fish until it flakes easily with a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh fish in the coldest part of the refrigerator and cook it within one to two days. For longer storage, wrap it tightly and freeze it. Thaw frozen fish in the refrigerator. Cooked fish should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within about three days. Unopened canned fish can be stored in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Guisada is a traditional Mexican stew made with slow‑cooked beef in a sauce of tomatoes, chilies, spices and aromatic herbs. The meat becomes tender while the sauce develops a rich, slightly spicy and fragrant flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Guisada is often prepared in clay pots (cazuelas), which enhance the aroma.
Classic recipes include bay leaves and cinnamon, giving the dish its characteristic Mexican scent.
The dish is especially popular in the Yucatán and Oaxaca regions, where it is served with corn tortillas.
In some areas guisada is accompanied by rice, beans and a squeeze of lime.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron and zinc, supporting immunity and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Guisada supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish fits low‑carb diets because its calories come mainly from protein and fat.

items.title: Beneficial plant compounds
items.content: Tomatoes, chilies and spices add antioxidants such as lycopene and capsaicin.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Slow‑cooked beef can contain notable amounts of saturated fat; people with heart disease should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: The sauce often includes added salt or soy sauce, raising the sodium content.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chilies, coriander or cumin.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: Rich meat can be heavy on the stomach for those with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot guisada with tortillas, rice or corn grits. Add fresh lime juice, cilantro and sliced avocado for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked guisada in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Hazelnuts are the fruits of the cultivated hazel (Corylus avellana), native to Europe and Western Asia. They have a crunchy texture and a mild, slightly sweet nutty flavor. Hazelnuts are eaten raw and roasted and added to baked goods, chocolate, spreads, salads, and porridge.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The world's largest producer of hazelnuts is Turkey.
The hazel blooms in late winter or early spring with catkins before its leaves appear.
The hazel grows as a shrub or small tree.
Hazelnuts are widely used in chocolate, praline, and nut spreads.
After roasting hazelnuts, the skins are easy to remove by rubbing the nuts in a towel.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: These fats can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contain vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contain magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contain manganese and folate
items.content: These nutrients play a role in metabolism and cell formation.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Hazelnuts can cause allergic reactions, sometimes severe; they are also linked to birch pollen allergy.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Hazelnuts are high in calories, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole hazelnuts are not suitable for small children because they can choke on them.

items.title: Mold
items.content: Nuts with mold or a bitter taste should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat hazelnuts as a snack, or add them to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, and desserts, or grind them into flour and spreads. To bring out the flavor, lightly roast them in the oven until golden, and remove the skins by rubbing them in a towel. Unsalted hazelnuts are the better choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hazelnuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place; in the shell they keep longer. Keep shelled hazelnuts in the refrigerator or freezer, because the fats can turn rancid. Discard nuts that smell rancid, taste bitter, or are moldy.

content.title: About
content.content: A turkey hot dog is a sausage made from turkey meat served in a soft bun. Turkey provides a milder flavor and lower fat content compared with traditional beef hot dogs, making it a lighter snack option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey contains roughly half the calories of beef for the same serving size while delivering similar protein.
The hot dog tradition started in the United States in the late 19th century; turkey versions have become popular in health‑focused diets.
Turkey is rich in tryptophan, an amino acid that supports serotonin production.
Some markets offer whole‑grain buns to boost the nutritional profile of the snack.
Turkey hot dogs are often served with mustard, ketchup, or low‑sugar barbecue sauce.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Turkey meat contains less saturated fat, helping to maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A single turkey hot dog provides about 15‑20 g of protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Moderate calorie count
items.content: One turkey hot dog typically contains 250‑300 kcal, suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed turkey sausages often contain added salt, so people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain products may contain nitrites or other preservatives, which should be limited.

items.title: Gluten in the bun
items.content: Standard buns contain gluten, making the snack unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the hot dog in the microwave or on a grill, split the bun, add mustard, ketchup, fresh veggies or slaw. It pairs well with fries or a cabbage salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated hot dogs at 0‑4 °C for up to 3 days. Frozen versions can be stored for up to 2 months in an airtight package.

content.title: About
content.content: Kung Pao Beef is a Sichuan Chinese dish featuring tender strips of beef stir‑fried with peanuts, vegetables, and a flavorful sauce made from soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, dried chilies and Sichuan peppercorns. The dish balances spicy, slightly sweet and nutty notes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Chinese words “Kung” (pepper) and “Pao” (stir‑fry).
While traditional recipes use beef, many variations use chicken, pork or tofu.
Sichuan peppercorn creates a characteristic “numbing” sensation on the palate.
Peanuts are added at the end of cooking to keep them crunchy.
The dish is commonly served with rice or noodles to temper the heat.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from beef supports hemoglobin levels and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies B12, B6 and niacin, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Sichuan pepper and ginger contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Healthy fats from peanuts
items.content: Peanuts add monounsaturated fats that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the peanuts used in the dish.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce contributes a significant amount of salt; people monitoring sodium intake should consume in moderation.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Sichuan pepper and dried chilies make the dish very hot; those with sensitive stomachs may want to reduce the spice level.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Peanuts and cooking oil increase the calorie count of the dish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Kung Pao Beef hot, typically over steamed rice or noodles. Fresh vegetables such as bell pepper or green onions can be added for extra crunch and color.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat with a splash of oil to restore the peanuts’ crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Light mayonnaise is a reduced‑fat dressing, typically containing 5‑10 % fat compared with traditional mayonnaise (≈70 %). It is made from vegetable oils, egg yolk, vinegar or lemon juice, flavorings and stabilizers. The product retains a creamy texture and characteristic taste while providing fewer calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light mayonnaise is widely used in diet‑focused meals and fast‑food restaurants.
To lower calories, part of the oil is replaced with water or low‑fat dairy ingredients.
In some countries light mayonnaise is mandatory in school cafeterias to limit fat intake.
It can be produced with olive, sunflower or rapeseed oil, each giving a distinct flavor profile.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Reduced fat helps lower the overall caloric density of meals, supporting weight management.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: The vegetable oils provide vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains omega‑6
items.content: Light mayonnaise supplies linoleic acid, essential for healthy skin and immune function.

items.title: Enhances flavor without excess calories
items.content: Its creamy texture and mild tang allow use in salads, sandwiches and sauces without adding many calories.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional light mayonnaise contains egg yolk, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some industrial versions may contain small amounts of trans fats – these should be limited.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt is added for taste; individuals with hypertension should monitor their intake.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Light mayonnaise is suitable for dressing salads, making sandwiches, sauces, marinades, and as a base for dips. It can be blended with mustard, yogurt or herbs to create varied flavors.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in the original container. After opening, consume within 1‑2 weeks. Discard if the smell, color or texture changes.
